newsitem.title: FRANCE: French judge gets secret bugging files.
newsitem.headline: French judge gets secret bugging files.

text.p: French conservative ex-premier Alain Juppe, in a last-minute decision before his election defeat, handed a magistrate hitherto secret files on illegal wiretapping under the late Socialist president Francois Mitterrand, officials said on Thursday.
They confirmed a report by the daily Le Monde that Juppe ordered the counter-intelligence agency DST last week to hand over "almost all" the files to investigating magistrate Jean-Michel Charpier.

Juppe had previously said the files were covered by state secrecy. They contain information on journalists, lawyers and politicians whose telephones conversations were monitored in 1982-1986 by Mitterrand's anti-terrorism unit.
The files were found in a garage rented by the former chief of the disbanded anti-terrorism unit, Christian Prouteau.

The head of the state watchdog on wiretaps, Paul Bouchet, told Reuters Juppe had asked him to sort out which ones must be covered by state secrecy, and both agreed that most could not because it would mean covering up illicit acts.

Only two of the documents would remain secret and be destroyed because they related to wiretaps legally ordered by the prime minister's office. Prouteau was formally placed under investigation on suspicion of stealing them.

Le Monde said the files were handed over to Charpier last Saturday, on the eve of a Socialist-led victory in parliamentary elections, and after the conservative Juppe said he would resign whatever the poll result.
Several people are under investigation over the wiretapping, including Gilles Menage, who headed Mitterrand's private office.
Juppe reacted angrily when Menage recently decided to breach state secrecy and answer magistrates' questions in order to defend himself from suspicion that he authorised the bugging.
Juppe then said only he could decide whether to lift state secrecy. He said that any wiretapping that followed legal procedures was covered by official secrecy and the rest was not.
